# Does an oil filter relocation increase the risk of a dry start?

Relocating an oil filter to facilitate maintenance is a common modification for heavy-duty applications, but the specific orientation you chooseâplacing the filter upside-down in the engine bayâintroduces a distinct hydraulic risk: a dry start. When a truck like the VG33E Nissan Xterra sits idle for an extended period, gravity dictates fluid behavior. If the filter element is oriented with its internal media facing downward and the housing open to the atmosphere, the lubricating oil will drain completely from the pleated element into the sump or drip onto the chassis.

The core issue isn't just that the oil leaves the canister; it is that the new orientation creates a scenario where the first few revolutions of the crankshaft occur with no hydraulic pressure support. In a standard installation, the filter remains full because the outlet restrictor (the spring-loaded bypass valve or the tight fit of the O-ring seal) prevents gravity from draining the fluid rapidly. However, an upside-down mount exposes the internal media to direct gravity drainage. As soon as the vehicle is tilted or started, the oil flows out until only the housing volume remains filled.

When you crank the engine after a long sit, the pump must spin the dry filter element before any oil can flow through the bypass valve into the gallery. This creates a temporary "dry start" condition where the rotating bearings and cam lobes experience metal-on-metal contact for the first few hundred RPMs until the sump pressure forces oil through the restricted inlet of the empty filter. While modern engines have robust designs, this transient lack of lubrication is unnecessary wear that can be mitigated by design or procedure.

To address this technically, you must consider how to maintain a fluid column within the new mounting position. One approach is to fill the relocated filter with oil before installation, ensuring it is full prior to connecting the line. This is feasible if the new location is accessible enough to pour oil into the canister via the cap opening. However, relying solely on this method introduces human error; if you forget to fill it during a routine service, the risk returns immediately.

A more robust engineering solution involves installing an anti-drainback valve within the filter housing itself or utilizing a check valve in the suction line connecting the engine block to the new location. In many aftermarket relocation kits, the bypass valve is integral to the element, but the housing geometry often lacks a dedicated anti-drainback mechanism if mounted upside down. You can fabricate a solution using a small reservoir tank situated near the ABS unit that feeds into the filter via a check valve, effectively creating a secondary oil supply that stays full regardless of gravity.

Alternatively, you could modify the mounting bracket to keep the inlet port facing upward relative to the engine, even if the body of the filter is inverted. This might require custom machining or 3D-printed adapters depending on the specific VG33E intake manifold clearance. The goal is to ensure that the suction line from the oil pump always sees a full canister of oil upon startup.

If you proceed with the relocation, verify that your new location does not introduce air pockets. Installing the filter upside down near the ABS unit requires careful routing of the feed line to prevent kinks or sharp bends that could trap air. Air in the lubrication system causes cavitation and reduces cooling efficiency, compounding the risks of a dry start.

Ultimately, if you cannot guarantee the filter remains full during long storage periods, an oil pressure switch wired directly to the ECU with a limp-home mode might be a necessary safety net. However, the simplest and most effective fix is to ensure the internal media never faces downward without a positive fill mechanism. The convenience of dropping the skid plate must not compromise the fundamental lubrication cycle of the engine block.
